expectedText:
GRANT DEED
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Morgan

GRANTING CLAUSE AND PROPERTY DECLARATION
Pat Morgan ("Grantor") hereby GRANTS to Jordan Morgan ("Grantee") all of Grantor's right, title, and interest in the real property located at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, together with all improvements, tenements, hereditaments, and appurtenances belonging to it. This deed's use of the word "grant" carries the statutory covenants and fee-simple presumption described elsewhere in this document. It is not a general warranty of title, and it does not by itself guarantee that Grantor holds any particular interest in the property beyond what those statutory covenants state.

LEGAL DESCRIPTION AND ASSESSOR'S PARCEL NUMBER
The real property this deed grants is more particularly described as follows, and this legal description controls if it differs from the street address given above: Lot 12, Block 3, Tract No. 4567, as per map recorded in Book 45, Page 12 of Maps, Sacramento County Records. This deed also references Assessor's Parcel Number 123-456-789, provided for identification only and not as part of the legal description.

THE STATUTORY GRANT DEED FORM AND FEE-SIMPLE PRESUMPTION
California's Civil Code sets out a statutory short form for "a grant of an estate in real property," built around the operative word "grant": "I, A B, grant to C D all that real property situated in (insert name of county) County, State of California, bounded (or described) as follows: ..." This deed, conveying the interest of Pat Morgan to Jordan Morgan in the real property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, uses that same operative word "grant." Separately, California law presumes that a grant of real property is intended to pass fee simple title — full ownership, rather than some lesser interest such as a life estate or a term of years — unless the grant itself shows that a lesser estate was intended.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "A grant of an estate in real property may be made in substance as follows: “I, A B, grant to C D all that real property situated in (insert name of county) County, State of California, bounded (or described) as follows: (here insert property description, or if the land sought to be conveyed has a descriptive name, it may be described by the name, as for instance, ‘The Norris Ranch.’) Witness my hand this (insert day) day of (insert month), 20___. _____ AB”"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1092, California Civil Code, statutory form of a grant of an estate in real property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1092.)
  "A fee simple title is presumed to be intended to pass by a grant of real property, unless it appears from the grant that a lesser estate was intended."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1105, California Civil Code, fee-simple title presumed from a grant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1105.)
  Known gap: §§ 1092 and 1105 are genuinely separate statutory sections within the same Civil Code chapter (Article 1, Mode of Transfer, and Article 2, Effect of Transfer, respectively), treated here as two independent sources. This is California's own statutory grant-deed form and fee-simple presumption, used as real evidence of how this state's law treats a conveyance that uses the word "grant" — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular transfer, or about whether another state uses the same terminology or presumption. § 1092's statutory form is optional wording ("may be made in substance as follows"); California law does not require a grant deed to track that exact form, only that it use operative language of grant, and this clause does not evaluate whether any particular deed's actual wording qualifies.

IMPLIED STATUTORY COVENANTS OF A GRANT DEED
Because this deed conveys Pat Morgan's interest in the real property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 using the word "grant," California law implies two specific covenants on Pat Morgan's part, running to Jordan Morgan and to Jordan Morgan's heirs and assigns, unless the deed's own express terms restrain them: first, that before signing this deed Pat Morgan has not already conveyed the same estate, or any right, title, or interest in it, to anyone other than Jordan Morgan; and second, that the estate is, as of the date this deed is signed, free from encumbrances done, made, or suffered by Pat Morgan or anyone claiming under Pat Morgan. California law states that these are the only covenants implied from the word "grant" — "the following covenants, and none other" — and that they may be sued upon in the same manner as if they had been expressly written into the deed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "From the use of the word “grant” in any conveyance by which an estate of inheritance or fee simple is to be passed, the following covenants, and none other, on the part of the grantor for himself and his heirs to the grantee, his heirs, and assigns, are implied, unless restrained by express terms contained in such conveyance: 1. That previous to the time of the execution of such conveyance, the grantor has not conveyed the same estate, or any right, title, or interest therein, to any person other than the grantee; 2. That such estate is at the time of the execution of such conveyance free from incumbrances done, made, or suffered by the grantor, or any person claiming under him. Such covenants may be sued upon in the same manner as if they had been expressly inserted in the conveyance."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1113, California Civil Code, covenants implied from the word "grant" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1113.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (§ 1113); no additional independent statutory source was found for these two implied covenants specifically, and that gap is disclosed here rather than filled with a second citation to a different subsection of the same section. This is California's own implied-covenant rule tied to the word "grant" — used as real evidence of what this state's law implies from that word — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular deed; which words of conveyance, if any, imply covenants of title, and what those covenants cover, vary from state to state. These statutory covenants are narrower than a general warranty of title: their text does not cover an encumbrance created by someone other than the grantor (for example, a prior owner), and it says nothing about matters of public record, boundary disputes, or title defects that do not arise from the grantor's own acts. This clause does not evaluate whether either covenant is in fact breached on the facts of any specific transfer.

AFTER-ACQUIRED TITLE PASSES AUTOMATICALLY
If Pat Morgan signs this deed purporting to grant the real property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 in fee simple, but does not yet hold full title to it at that time, and Pat Morgan later acquires title or a claim of title to that property, California law passes that later-acquired title automatically — by operation of law — to Jordan Morgan or Jordan Morgan's successors, without requiring Pat Morgan to sign a new deed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Where a person purports by proper instrument to grant real property in fee simple, and subsequently acquires any title, or claim of title thereto, the same passes by operation of law to the grantee, or his successors."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1106, California Civil Code, after-acquired title passes by operation of law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1106.)
  Known gap: The research brief that prompted this clause pointed to Civil Code § 1105 for the after-acquired-title rule. Direct review of the statutory text shows that citation is incorrect: § 1105 states a different rule — that a grant of real property is presumed to convey fee simple unless the grant shows a lesser estate was intended — and that rule is addressed in a separate clause. The after-acquired-title rule is instead stated in the next section, § 1106, quoted below; that correction is disclosed here rather than silently carried forward. This is a single statutory section (§ 1106); no additional independent statutory source was found for the after-acquired-title rule itself. This is California's own after-acquired-title rule, tied to an instrument that "purports to grant" property in fee simple, used as real evidence of how this state's law treats that situation — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular transfer or a particular grantor's later-acquired interest, and not every state applies an equivalent doctrine, or applies it identically, to every type of deed.

WRITING REQUIREMENT AND EXECUTION BY AN ATTORNEY IN FACT
California law requires that a transfer of an estate in real property — other than a lease for a term of one year or less — be made by a written instrument, signed by the person disposing of the interest, or by that person's agent if the agent is authorized to sign in writing. If Pat Morgan's deed is instead signed by an attorney in fact acting on Pat Morgan's behalf, California law requires the attorney in fact to sign both Pat Morgan's name as the principal and the attorney in fact's own name, identified as attorney in fact.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "An estate in real property, other than an estate at will or for a term not exceeding one year, can be transferred only by operation of law, or by an instrument in writing, subscribed by the party disposing of the same, or by his agent thereunto authorized by writing."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1091, California Civil Code, real property transfers must be in writing (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1091.)
  "When an attorney in fact executes an instrument transferring an estate in real property, he must subscribe the name of his principal to it, and his own name as attorney in fact."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1095, California Civil Code, execution by an attorney in fact (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1095.)
  Known gap: This states California's own writing and execution formalities for a transfer of real property generally; it is not specific to quitclaim deeds as a category, and it is not a claim about which state's execution formalities apply to a particular transfer — states differ on whether a deed must be witnessed, how an agent's authority must be documented, and similar mechanics. §§ 1091 and 1095 are genuinely separate statutory sections, treated here as two independent sources. This clause does not address the separate requirement — found in the Government Code, not the Civil Code — that a deed's execution be acknowledged before a notary public in order to be recorded; that requirement is addressed in a separate clause.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT BEFORE A NOTARY AND RECORDER ACCEPTANCE
For a deed to be recorded in California, its execution generally must be acknowledged by the person who signed it. A quitclaim deed is one of the specific instrument types California law does not allow to be recorded merely on "proof" by a subscribing witness in place of acknowledgment — a quitclaim deed's execution must be acknowledged before a notary public or other authorized officer, and that acknowledgment must itself be certified as prescribed by law. Separately, a county recorder must accept a properly acknowledged quitclaim deed for recordation, on payment of the proper fees and taxes, if it contains enough information to be indexed, meets state and local recording requirements, and is photographically reproducible; the recorder may not refuse to record it on the basis of its "lack of legal sufficiency."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Unless it belongs to the class provided for in either Sections 27282 to 27286, inclusive, or Section 1202 or 1203, of the Civil Code, or is a fictitious mortgage or deed of trust as provided in Section 2952 or 2963 of the Civil Code, or is a fictitious oil and gas lease as provided in Section 1219 of the Civil Code, or is a claim of lien under Section 8416 of the Civil Code or a notice of completion under Section 8182 or 9204 of the Civil Code, before an instrument can be recorded its execution shall be acknowledged by the person executing it, or if executed by a corporation, by its president or secretary or other person executing it on behalf of the corporation, or, except for any power of attorney, quitclaim deed, grant deed, mortgage, deed of trust, security agreement, or other document affecting real property, proved by subscribing witness or as provided in Sections 1198 and 1199 of the Civil Code, and the acknowledgment or proof certified as prescribed by law. This section shall not apply to a trustee’s deed resulting from a decree of foreclosure, or a nonjudicial foreclosure pursuant to Section 2924 of the Civil Code, or to a deed of reconveyance."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 27287, California Government Code, acknowledgment required before an instrument can be recorded (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=27287.)
  "The recorder shall, upon payment of proper fees and taxes, accept for recordation any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, or court order to be recorded, or authorized or required to be recorded by a local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property, if the instrument, paper, or notice contains sufficient information to be indexed as provided by statute, meets recording requirements of state statutes and local ordinances, and is photographically reproducible. The county recorder shall not refuse to record any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, court order, or local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property to be recorded on the basis of its lack of legal sufficiency."
  — Cal. Gov't Code § 27201(a)(1)(A), California Government Code, recorder's duty to accept a conforming instrument for recordation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=GOV&sectionNum=27201.)
  Known gap: This is California's own recording-formalities framework; acknowledgment and recording mechanics are not uniform across states, and this is not a claim about which state's law governs a particular deed. §§ 27287 and 27201 are genuinely separate Government Code sections, treated here as two independent sources. § 27201's "local recording requirements" language is a direct acknowledgment that individual county recorders impose their own additional formatting rules (margins, page size, first-page content, and similar mechanics) on top of this statewide framework; this clause does not catalog any specific county's additional requirements. Separately, this clause does not address the county documentary transfer tax or Preliminary Change of Ownership Report steps that commonly accompany recording a deed — those are addressed in separate clauses.

RECORDING: CONSTRUCTIVE NOTICE AND CALIFORNIA'S RACE-NOTICE RULE
A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest Pat Morgan has to Jordan Morgan once it is validly executed and delivered, even if it is never recorded; recording is not a condition of the deed's validity between Pat Morgan and Jordan Morgan. Recording matters for what it does against later claimants: once a conveyance of real property is acknowledged, certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, it serves as constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees, from the time it is filed with the recorder. California is a "race-notice" recording state — an earlier conveyance of the same property that is not recorded is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee who takes the property in good faith, for valuable consideration, and records first.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein acknowledged or proved and certified and recorded as prescribed by law from the time it is filed with the recorder for record is constructive notice of the contents thereof to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees; and a certified copy of such a recorded conveyance may be recorded in any other county and when so recorded the record thereof shall have the same force and effect as though it was of the original conveyance and where the original conveyance has been recorded in any county wherein the property therein mentioned is not situated a certified copy of the recorded conveyance may be recorded in the county where such property is situated with the same force and effect as if the original conveyance had been recorded in that county."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1213, California Civil Code, recording gives constructive notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1213.)
  "Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1214, California Civil Code, race-notice recording rule (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1214.)
  Known gap: California's race-notice recording rule is stated here as evidence of how one state resolves competing claims to the same property, not as a claim about which state's recording rule governs a particular property or transfer — recording statutes vary meaningfully by state, including "pure race" states (first to record wins regardless of notice) and "pure notice" states (a later good-faith purchaser without notice prevails even if they record second). §§ 1213 and 1214 are genuinely separate statutory sections, treated here as two independent sources. This clause does not evaluate whether a particular later claimant on the facts of any specific transfer actually qualifies as a good-faith purchaser for valuable consideration, and it does not address the documentary transfer tax or Preliminary Change of Ownership Report steps a county recorder may separately require at the time of recording — those are addressed in separate clauses.

PRELIMINARY CHANGE OF OWNERSHIP REPORT
California law directs each county assessor and recorder to make a "Preliminary Change of Ownership Report" form available, which the transferee of real property completes and may file with the recorder at the time a document effecting a change in ownership — such as this deed — is recorded. The report must be signed by the transferee personally, or by an officer of a transferee entity, certifying that the information given is true, correct, and complete to the best of the transferee's knowledge; an agent acting for the transferee may not sign it. If a deed is presented for recording without a report filed concurrently, the recorder may charge an additional recording fee, but noncompliance does not otherwise delay or block recording once that fee is paid. Separately, certain transfers between spouses do not count as a taxable "change in ownership" in the first place, including a transfer that creates, transfers, or terminates a co-owner's interest solely between spouses, and a transfer to a spouse in connection with a marital settlement agreement or a dissolution or legal-separation judgment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) Each county assessor and recorder shall make available, without charge and upon request, a form entitled “Preliminary Change of Ownership Report,” which transferees of real property shall complete and may file with the recorder concurrent with the recordation of any document effecting a change in ownership. The form shall be signed by the transferee or an officer of the transferee certifying that the information provided on the form is, to the best of his or her knowledge and belief, true, correct, and complete. The form shall not be signed by an agent acting for a transferee. (b) If a document evidencing a change in ownership is presented to the recorder for recordation without the concurrent filing of a preliminary change in ownership report, the recorder may charge an additional recording fee of twenty dollars ($20). (c) Noncompliance with this section by the transferee shall not delay or preclude the recordation of documents if the additional fee specified in subdivision (b) is tendered."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 480.3(a)-(c), California Revenue and Taxation Code, Preliminary Change of Ownership Report (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=480.3.)
  "Notwithstanding any other provision in this chapter, a change of ownership shall not include any interspousal transfer, including, but not limited to: (a) Transfers to a trustee for the beneficial use of a spouse, or the surviving spouse of a deceased transferor, or by a trustee of such a trust to the spouse of the trustor, (b) Transfers which take effect upon the death of a spouse, (c) Transfers to a spouse or former spouse in connection with a property settlement agreement or decree of dissolution of a marriage or legal separation, or (d) The creation, transfer, or termination, solely between spouses, of any coowner’s interest. (e) The distribution of a legal entity’s property to a spouse or former spouse in exchange for the interest of such spouse in the legal entity in connection with a property settlement agreement or a decree of dissolution of a marriage or legal separation."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 63, California Revenue and Taxation Code, interspousal transfers excluded from "change in ownership" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=63.)
  Known gap: This states two genuinely separate California statutory sections — § 480.3, governing the PCOR filing mechanic and fee, and § 63, defining an interspousal exclusion from what counts as a taxable "change in ownership" — treated here as independent sources. Whether a particular transfer this deed effects falls inside that interspousal exclusion depends on facts (who the parties are, what interest passes, and why) that this clause does not evaluate for any specific transfer. Being excluded from "change in ownership" for reassessment purposes is not necessarily the same as being excused from filing a PCOR at all — county assessor practice commonly still expects a report to be filed, or a specific exemption to be claimed on it, even for an excluded transfer; this clause states that distinction rather than resolving it. This is California's own reporting regime; other states do not necessarily use an equivalent form or filing mechanic, and this is not a claim about which state's law applies to a given transfer. This clause does not address the separate documentary transfer tax, covered in another clause.

COUNTY DOCUMENTARY TRANSFER TAX AND COMMON EXEMPTIONS
California law authorizes — it does not itself directly impose — a county documentary transfer tax on a deed by which real property is granted, assigned, transferred, or otherwise conveyed, when the consideration or value of the interest conveyed exceeds $100. A county that adopts the tax by ordinance may charge $0.55 per $500 (or fractional part) of that consideration or value; a city within that county may separately adopt, by its own ordinance, up to half that rate on the same transfer. Two exemptions commonly relevant to a quitclaim deed exist in the statute: a deed that divides or allocates community, quasi-community, or quasi-marital property between spouses under, or in contemplation of, a dissolution or legal-separation judgment is exempt if the deed includes a written recital, signed by either spouse, stating that it is entitled to the exemption; and a deed made as an inter vivos gift, or by reason of death — including a transfer outright to, or in trust for the benefit of, any person or entity — is exempt as well.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(a) The board of supervisors of any county or city and county, by an ordinance adopted pursuant to this part, may impose, on each deed, instrument, or writing by which any lands, tenements, or other realty sold within the county shall be granted, assigned, transferred, or otherwise conveyed to, or vested in, the purchaser or purchasers, or any other person or persons, by his or their direction, when the consideration or value of the interest or property conveyed (exclusive of the value of any lien or encumbrance remaining thereon at the time of sale) exceeds one hundred dollars ($100) a tax at the rate of fifty-five cents ($0.55) for each five hundred dollars ($500) or fractional part thereof. (b) The legislative body of any city which is within a county which has imposed a tax pursuant to subdivision (a) may, by an ordinance adopted pursuant to this part, impose, on each deed, instrument, or writing by which any lands, tenements, or other realty sold within the city shall be granted, assigned, transferred, or otherwise conveyed to, or vested in, the purchaser or purchasers, or any other person or persons, by his or their direction, when the consideration or value of the interest or property conveyed (exclusive of the value of any lien or encumbrance remaining thereon at the time of sale) exceeds one hundred dollars ($100), a tax at the rate of one-half the amount specified in subdivision (a) for each five hundred dollars ($500) or fractional part thereof. (c) A credit shall be allowed against the tax imposed by a county ordinance pursuant to subdivision (a) for the amount of any tax due to any city by reason of an ordinance adopted pursuant to subdivision (b). No credit shall be allowed against any county tax for a city tax which is not in conformity with this part."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 11911, California Revenue and Taxation Code, county (and city) documentary transfer tax (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=11911.)
  "(a) Any tax imposed pursuant to this part shall not apply with respect to any deed, instrument, or other writing which purports to transfer, divide, or allocate community, quasi-community, or quasi-marital property assets between spouses for the purpose of effecting a division of community, quasi-community, or quasi-marital property which is required by a judgment decreeing a dissolution of the marriage or legal separation, by a judgment of nullity, or by any other judgment or order rendered pursuant to the Family Code, or by a written agreement between the spouses, executed in contemplation of any such judgment or order, whether or not the written agreement is incorporated as part of any of those judgments or orders. (b) In order to qualify for the exemption provided in subdivision (a), the deed, instrument, or other writing shall include a written recital, signed by either spouse, stating that the deed, instrument, or other writing is entitled to the exemption."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 11927, California Revenue and Taxation Code, marital-dissolution exemption from the transfer tax (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=11927.)
  "Any tax imposed pursuant to this part shall not apply to any deed, instrument, or other writing which purports to grant, assign, transfer, convey, divide, allocate, or vest lands, tenements, or realty, or any interest therein, if by reason of such inter vivos gift or by reason of the death of any person, such lands, tenements, realty, or interests therein are transferred outright to, or in trust for the benefit of, any person or entity."
  — Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 11930, California Revenue and Taxation Code, gift exemption from the transfer tax (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=RTC&sectionNum=11930.)
  Known gap: This states three genuinely separate sections of California's Documentary Transfer Tax Act — § 11911 (the tax itself), § 11927 (the marital-dissolution exemption), and § 11930 (the gift exemption) — treated here as three independent sources. This is not a complete list of every exemption in that Act; other exemptions exist for transaction types (for example, certain entity reorganizations and refinancings) not addressed here, and this clause does not determine whether a particular transfer, on its own facts, actually qualifies for either exemption described. Importantly, this statute is only the statewide/county documentary transfer tax framework: many California cities impose their own additional documentary transfer tax, and for some charter cities that additional tax has been adopted by voter initiative at rates and under authority that go beyond the half-of-the-county-rate structure that § 11911(b) itself describes for a general-law city. This document addresses the statewide/county documentary transfer tax framework only, not any particular city's additional tax, and is not a claim about which state's transfer-tax law applies to a given transfer.

SIGNATURE, NOTARIAL ACKNOWLEDGMENT, AND RECORDING
SIGNATURE AND DATE: Pat Morgan signs and dates this deed below; the name should exactly match the name shown on the property's current title documents.

Signature of Pat Morgan: _________________________ Date: _______________

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF NOTARY: A notary public or other officer completing this certificate verifies only the identity of the individual who signed the document to which this certificate is attached, and not the truthfulness, accuracy, or validity of that document.

State of California ) County of _________________________ )

On _________________________ before me, _________________________ (here insert name and title of the officer), personally appeared _________________________, who proved to me on the basis of satisfactory evidence to be the person(s) whose name(s) is/are subscribed to the within instrument and acknowledged to me that they executed the same in their authorized capacity(ies), and that by their signature(s) on the instrument the person(s), or the entity upon behalf of which the person(s) acted, executed the instrument. I certify under PENALTY OF PERJURY under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing paragraph is true and correct.

WITNESS my hand and official seal.

Signature: _________________________ (Seal)

RECORDING: This deed transfers Pat Morgan's interest, together with the statutory covenants described above, to Jordan Morgan once it is validly signed and delivered; it is not recorded automatically upon signing. Recording is a separate step: presenting the signed, notarized deed to the county recorder in the county where the property is located, together with any required Preliminary Change of Ownership Report and any applicable documentary transfer tax.

citations.quote: From the use of the word “grant” in any conveyance by which an estate of inheritance or fee simple is to be passed, the following covenants, and none other, on the part of the grantor for himself and his heirs to the grantee, his heirs, and assigns, are implied, unless restrained by express terms contained in such conveyance: 1. That previous to the time of the execution of such conveyance, the grantor has not conveyed the same estate, or any right, title, or interest therein, to any person other than the grantee; 2. That such estate is at the time of the execution of such conveyance free from incumbrances done, made, or suffered by the grantor, or any person claiming under him. Such covenants may be sued upon in the same manner as if they had been expressly inserted in the conveyance.

This is California's own implied-covenant rule tied to the word "grant" — used as real evidence of what this state's law implies from that word — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular deed; which words of conveyance, if any, imply covenants of title, and what those covenants cover, vary from state to state. These statutory covenants are narrower than a general warranty of title: their text does not cover an encumbrance created by someone other than the grantor (for example, a prior owner), and it says nothing about matters of public record, boundary disputes, or title defects that do not arise from the grantor's own acts. This clause does not evaluate whether either covenant is in fact breached on the facts of any specific transfer.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, after-acquired title passes by operation of law
citations.quote: Where a person purports by proper instrument to grant real property in fee simple, and subsequently acquires any title, or claim of title thereto, the same passes by operation of law to the grantee, or his successors.

expectedJSON.body: California law requires that a transfer of an estate in real property — other than a lease for a term of one year or less — be made by a written instrument, signed by the person disposing of the interest, or by that person's agent if the agent is authorized to sign in writing. If Pat Morgan's deed is instead signed by an attorney in fact acting on Pat Morgan's behalf, California law requires the attorney in fact to sign both Pat Morgan's name as the principal and the attorney in fact's own name, identified as attorney in fact.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, real property transfers must be in writing
citations.quote: An estate in real property, other than an estate at will or for a term not exceeding one year, can be transferred only by operation of law, or by an instrument in writing, subscribed by the party disposing of the same, or by his agent thereunto authorized by writing.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, execution by an attorney in fact
citations.quote: When an attorney in fact executes an instrument transferring an estate in real property, he must subscribe the name of his principal to it, and his own name as attorney in fact.

This clause does not address the separate requirement — found in the Government Code, not the Civil Code — that a deed's execution be acknowledged before a notary public in order to be recorded; that requirement is addressed in a separate clause.

expectedJSON.body: For a deed to be recorded in California, its execution generally must be acknowledged by the person who signed it. A quitclaim deed is one of the specific instrument types California law does not allow to be recorded merely on "proof" by a subscribing witness in place of acknowledgment — a quitclaim deed's execution must be acknowledged before a notary public or other authorized officer, and that acknowledgment must itself be certified as prescribed by law. Separately, a county recorder must accept a properly acknowledged quitclaim deed for recordation, on payment of the proper fees and taxes, if it contains enough information to be indexed, meets state and local recording requirements, and is photographically reproducible; the recorder may not refuse to record it on the basis of its "lack of legal sufficiency."

citations.cite: California Government Code, acknowledgment required before an instrument can be recorded
citations.quote: Unless it belongs to the class provided for in either Sections 27282 to 27286, inclusive, or Section 1202 or 1203, of the Civil Code, or is a fictitious mortgage or deed of trust as provided in Section 2952 or 2963 of the Civil Code, or is a fictitious oil and gas lease as provided in Section 1219 of the Civil Code, or is a claim of lien under Section 8416 of the Civil Code or a notice of completion under Section 8182 or 9204 of the Civil Code, before an instrument can be recorded its execution shall be acknowledged by the person executing it, or if executed by a corporation, by its president or secretary or other person executing it on behalf of the corporation, or, except for any power of attorney, quitclaim deed, grant deed, mortgage, deed of trust, security agreement, or other document affecting real property, proved by subscribing witness or as provided in Sections 1198 and 1199 of the Civil Code, and the acknowledgment or proof certified as prescribed by law. This section shall not apply to a trustee’s deed resulting from a decree of foreclosure, or a nonjudicial foreclosure pursuant to Section 2924 of the Civil Code, or to a deed of reconveyance.

citations.cite: California Government Code, recorder's duty to accept a conforming instrument for recordation
citations.quote: The recorder shall, upon payment of proper fees and taxes, accept for recordation any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, or court order to be recorded, or authorized or required to be recorded by a local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property, if the instrument, paper, or notice contains sufficient information to be indexed as provided by statute, meets recording requirements of state statutes and local ordinances, and is photographically reproducible. The county recorder shall not refuse to record any instrument, paper, or notice that is authorized or required by statute, court order, or local ordinance that relates to the recordation of any instrument, paper, or notice that relates to real property to be recorded on the basis of its lack of legal sufficiency.

expectedJSON.body: A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest Pat Morgan has to Jordan Morgan once it is validly executed and delivered, even if it is never recorded; recording is not a condition of the deed's validity between Pat Morgan and Jordan Morgan. Recording matters for what it does against later claimants: once a conveyance of real property is acknowledged, certified, and recorded as prescribed by law, it serves as constructive notice of its contents to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees, from the time it is filed with the recorder. California is a "race-notice" recording state — an earlier conveyance of the same property that is not recorded is void against a later purchaser or mortgagee who takes the property in good faith, for valuable consideration, and records first.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, recording gives constructive notice
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein acknowledged or proved and certified and recorded as prescribed by law from the time it is filed with the recorder for record is constructive notice of the contents thereof to subsequent purchasers and mortgagees; and a certified copy of such a recorded conveyance may be recorded in any other county and when so recorded the record thereof shall have the same force and effect as though it was of the original conveyance and where the original conveyance has been recorded in any county wherein the property therein mentioned is not situated a certified copy of the recorded conveyance may be recorded in the county where such property is situated with the same force and effect as if the original conveyance had been recorded in that county.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, race-notice recording rule
citations.quote: Every conveyance of real property or an estate for years therein, other than a lease for a term not exceeding one year, is void as against any subsequent purchaser or mortgagee of the same property, or any part thereof, in good faith and for a valuable consideration, whose conveyance is first duly recorded, and as against any judgment affecting the title, unless the conveyance shall have been duly recorded prior to the record of notice of action.

expectedJSON.gap: California's race-notice recording rule is stated here as evidence of how one state resolves competing claims to the same property, not as a claim about which state's recording rule governs a particular property or transfer — recording statutes vary meaningfully by state, including "pure race" states (first to record wins regardless of notice) and "pure notice" states (a later good-faith purchaser without notice prevails even if they record second). §§ 1213 and 1214 are genuinely separate statutory sections, treated here as two independent sources. This clause does not evaluate whether a particular later claimant on the facts of any specific transfer actually qualifies as a good-faith purchaser for valuable consideration, and it does not address the documentary transfer tax or Preliminary Change of Ownership Report steps a county recorder may separately require at the time of recording — those are addressed in separate clauses.

expectedJSON.body: California law directs each county assessor and recorder to make a "Preliminary Change of Ownership Report" form available, which the transferee of real property completes and may file with the recorder at the time a document effecting a change in ownership — such as this deed — is recorded. The report must be signed by the transferee personally, or by an officer of a transferee entity, certifying that the information given is true, correct, and complete to the best of the transferee's knowledge; an agent acting for the transferee may not sign it. If a deed is presented for recording without a report filed concurrently, the recorder may charge an additional recording fee, but noncompliance does not otherwise delay or block recording once that fee is paid. Separately, certain transfers between spouses do not count as a taxable "change in ownership" in the first place, including a transfer that creates, transfers, or terminates a co-owner's interest solely between spouses, and a transfer to a spouse in connection with a marital settlement agreement or a dissolution or legal-separation judgment.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, Preliminary Change of Ownership Report
citations.quote: (a) Each county assessor and recorder shall make available, without charge and upon request, a form entitled “Preliminary Change of Ownership Report,” which transferees of real property shall complete and may file with the recorder concurrent with the recordation of any document effecting a change in ownership. The form shall be signed by the transferee or an officer of the transferee certifying that the information provided on the form is, to the best of his or her knowledge and belief, true, correct, and complete. The form shall not be signed by an agent acting for a transferee. (b) If a document evidencing a change in ownership is presented to the recorder for recordation without the concurrent filing of a preliminary change in ownership report, the recorder may charge an additional recording fee of twenty dollars ($20). (c) Noncompliance with this section by the transferee shall not delay or preclude the recordation of documents if the additional fee specified in subdivision (b) is tendered.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, interspousal transfers excluded from "change in ownership"
citations.quote: Notwithstanding any other provision in this chapter, a change of ownership shall not include any interspousal transfer, including, but not limited to: (a) Transfers to a trustee for the beneficial use of a spouse, or the surviving spouse of a deceased transferor, or by a trustee of such a trust to the spouse of the trustor, (b) Transfers which take effect upon the death of a spouse, (c) Transfers to a spouse or former spouse in connection with a property settlement agreement or decree of dissolution of a marriage or legal separation, or (d) The creation, transfer, or termination, solely between spouses, of any coowner’s interest. (e) The distribution of a legal entity’s property to a spouse or former spouse in exchange for the interest of such spouse in the legal entity in connection with a property settlement agreement or a decree of dissolution of a marriage or legal separation.

expectedJSON.gap: This states two genuinely separate California statutory sections — § 480.3, governing the PCOR filing mechanic and fee, and § 63, defining an interspousal exclusion from what counts as a taxable "change in ownership" — treated here as independent sources. Whether a particular transfer this deed effects falls inside that interspousal exclusion depends on facts (who the parties are, what interest passes, and why) that this clause does not evaluate for any specific transfer. Being excluded from "change in ownership" for reassessment purposes is not necessarily the same as being excused from filing a PCOR at all — county assessor practice commonly still expects a report to be filed, or a specific exemption to be claimed on it, even for an excluded transfer; this clause states that distinction rather than resolving it. This is California's own reporting regime; other states do not necessarily use an equivalent form or filing mechanic, and this is not a claim about which state's law applies to a given transfer. This clause does not address the separate documentary transfer tax, covered in another clause.

expectedJSON.body: California law authorizes — it does not itself directly impose — a county documentary transfer tax on a deed by which real property is granted, assigned, transferred, or otherwise conveyed, when the consideration or value of the interest conveyed exceeds $100. A county that adopts the tax by ordinance may charge $0.55 per $500 (or fractional part) of that consideration or value; a city within that county may separately adopt, by its own ordinance, up to half that rate on the same transfer. Two exemptions commonly relevant to a quitclaim deed exist in the statute: a deed that divides or allocates community, quasi-community, or quasi-marital property between spouses under, or in contemplation of, a dissolution or legal-separation judgment is exempt if the deed includes a written recital, signed by either spouse, stating that it is entitled to the exemption; and a deed made as an inter vivos gift, or by reason of death — including a transfer outright to, or in trust for the benefit of, any person or entity — is exempt as well.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, county (and city) documentary transfer tax
citations.quote: (a) The board of supervisors of any county or city and county, by an ordinance adopted pursuant to this part, may impose, on each deed, instrument, or writing by which any lands, tenements, or other realty sold within the county shall be granted, assigned, transferred, or otherwise conveyed to, or vested in, the purchaser or purchasers, or any other person or persons, by his or their direction, when the consideration or value of the interest or property conveyed (exclusive of the value of any lien or encumbrance remaining thereon at the time of sale) exceeds one hundred dollars ($100) a tax at the rate of fifty-five cents ($0.55) for each five hundred dollars ($500) or fractional part thereof. (b) The legislative body of any city which is within a county which has imposed a tax pursuant to subdivision (a) may, by an ordinance adopted pursuant to this part, impose, on each deed, instrument, or writing by which any lands, tenements, or other realty sold within the city shall be granted, assigned, transferred, or otherwise conveyed to, or vested in, the purchaser or purchasers, or any other person or persons, by his or their direction, when the consideration or value of the interest or property conveyed (exclusive of the value of any lien or encumbrance remaining thereon at the time of sale) exceeds one hundred dollars ($100), a tax at the rate of one-half the amount specified in subdivision (a) for each five hundred dollars ($500) or fractional part thereof. (c) A credit shall be allowed against the tax imposed by a county ordinance pursuant to subdivision (a) for the amount of any tax due to any city by reason of an ordinance adopted pursuant to subdivision (b). No credit shall be allowed against any county tax for a city tax which is not in conformity with this part.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, marital-dissolution exemption from the transfer tax
citations.quote: (a) Any tax imposed pursuant to this part shall not apply with respect to any deed, instrument, or other writing which purports to transfer, divide, or allocate community, quasi-community, or quasi-marital property assets between spouses for the purpose of effecting a division of community, quasi-community, or quasi-marital property which is required by a judgment decreeing a dissolution of the marriage or legal separation, by a judgment of nullity, or by any other judgment or order rendered pursuant to the Family Code, or by a written agreement between the spouses, executed in contemplation of any such judgment or order, whether or not the written agreement is incorporated as part of any of those judgments or orders. (b) In order to qualify for the exemption provided in subdivision (a), the deed, instrument, or other writing shall include a written recital, signed by either spouse, stating that the deed, instrument, or other writing is entitled to the exemption.

citations.cite: California Revenue and Taxation Code, gift exemption from the transfer tax
citations.quote: Any tax imposed pursuant to this part shall not apply to any deed, instrument, or other writing which purports to grant, assign, transfer, convey, divide, allocate, or vest lands, tenements, or realty, or any interest therein, if by reason of such inter vivos gift or by reason of the death of any person, such lands, tenements, realty, or interests therein are transferred outright to, or in trust for the benefit of, any person or entity.

expectedJSON.gap: This states three genuinely separate sections of California's Documentary Transfer Tax Act — § 11911 (the tax itself), § 11927 (the marital-dissolution exemption), and § 11930 (the gift exemption) — treated here as three independent sources. This is not a complete list of every exemption in that Act; other exemptions exist for transaction types (for example, certain entity reorganizations and refinancings) not addressed here, and this clause does not determine whether a particular transfer, on its own facts, actually qualifies for either exemption described. Importantly, this statute is only the statewide/county documentary transfer tax framework: many California cities impose their own additional documentary transfer tax, and for some charter cities that additional tax has been adopted by voter initiative at rates and under authority that go beyond the half-of-the-county-rate structure that § 11911(b) itself describes for a general-law city. This document addresses the statewide/county documentary transfer tax framework only, not any particular city's additional tax, and is not a claim about which state's transfer-tax law applies to a given transfer.
